\chapter{The Room You Are In}
\label{ch:ta-the-room-you-are-in}
\hlchaptermodality{70}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name a table, a bed, a wall, the floor and a roof in Tamil, and place each one against a direction I already know.}

Complete TA-C70-roof and say all five words of the chapter in order.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[mēsai]{\ta{மேசை} (mēsai) — a table}

\label{lesson:TA-C70-table}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{nilaiyam} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{மேசை}}
\textbf{\ta{மேசை}} (\emph{mēsai}) — \textquotedblleft{}a table\textquotedblright{}.

The table you eat at, or write at.

Put it beside \ta{நாற்காலி} (\emph{nāṟkāli}), the chair you already have — the word you could take apart into \textquotedblleft{}four\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}leg\textquotedblright{}. A \ta{மேசை} and a \ta{நாற்காலி} are the pair a room is furnished with, and now you can name both.

Its two signs are old friends: the \textbf{\ta{ே}} in front of \ta{ம}, and the \textbf{\ta{ை}} at the end.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first thing in the room.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{mēsai}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{nāṟkāli}, then \emph{mēsai} — the pair, in the order you sit down to them
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{sālai}, then say \emph{nilaiyam}, then say \emph{mēsai}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ta{மேசை} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}A table\textquotedblright{}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kaṭṭil]{\ta{கட்டில்} (kaṭṭil) — a bed}

\label{lesson:TA-C70-bed}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{mēsai} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{கட்டில்}}
\textbf{\ta{கட்டில்}} (\emph{kaṭṭil}) — \textquotedblleft{}a bed\textquotedblright{}.

A bed — and in Tamil it is named as a \textbf{made thing}: a frame with cords or webbing tied across it.

You already have \ta{தூக்கம்} (\emph{tūkkam}), sleep. The pair is easy to hold: the \ta{தூக்கம்} happens on the \ta{கட்டில்}.

Its middle is the doubled \textbf{\ta{ட்ட}} you took apart in \ta{சட்டை}, and it closes on \textbf{\ta{ல்}} — a letter with the vowel taken off, exactly like the \ta{ண்} in \ta{வண்டி}, except that here there is nothing after it to lean on.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two, and you can now name where you sleep.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{kaṭṭil}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{tūkkam}, then \emph{kaṭṭil} — the thing and the place
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{nilaiyam}, then say \emph{mēsai}, then say \emph{kaṭṭil}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where does the \ta{தூக்கம்} happen? (On the \textbf{\ta{கட்டில்}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[mēsai]{\ta{மேசை} — two front-hanging signs in one word}

\label{lesson:TA-W26-read-mesai}



\begin{quote}
Before the page: you can say \emph{mēsai} and \emph{kaṭṭil}. Now read the first one.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \ta{மேசை} — two front-hanging signs in one word}
\textbf{\ta{மேசை}} is the first word you have read that carries a front-hanging sign on \textbf{each} of its two letters.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{piece} & \textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ta{மே}} & \emph{mē} & \ta{ம} with the \textbf{\ta{ே}} sign, the one you read twice in \ta{மேலே} \\
\textbf{\ta{சை}} & \emph{sai} & \ta{ச} with the \textbf{\ta{ை}} sign, the one you read at the end of \ta{சட்டை} and \ta{கடை} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ta{மே} · \ta{சை} $\to$ \ta{மேசை}}
\end{quote}

Both signs are drawn to the \textbf{left} of their letter and said \textbf{after} it. So the eye moves left-to-right across four marks while the mouth says only two beats, and the order of the two is not the order they were printed in. Read it slowly once and let that happen on purpose.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Read it:} \textbf{\ta{மே}} — then \textbf{\ta{சை}} — then \textbf{\ta{மேசை}}
  \item \emph{Point to:} both signs, and say which side of their letters they sit on
  \item \emph{Read it:} \textbf{\ta{மேலே}}, then \textbf{\ta{மேசை}}, and find the sign they share
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{mēsai}, then say \emph{kaṭṭil}, then read \textbf{\ta{மேசை}}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Read \textbf{\ta{மேசை}}. How many signs does it carry, and are they said before or after their letters? (\textbf{Two}; \textbf{after}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[suvar]{\ta{சுவர்} (suvar) — a wall}

\label{lesson:TA-C70-wall}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: read \textbf{\ta{மேசை}}, and say what it means.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{சுவர்}}
\textbf{\ta{சுவர்}} (\emph{suvar}) — \textquotedblleft{}a wall\textquotedblright{}.

The wall of a room or a house.

It is short and it is bare — two letters and a closing \textbf{\ta{ர்}}, no vowel signs hanging off the front of anything. Words shaped this plainly are usually old ones, and this is one of them.

It is also the surface that makes \ta{உள்ளே} and \ta{வெளியே} mean anything: a \ta{சுவர்} is what there is an inside and an outside of.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three, and the room has an edge.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{suvar}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{suvar}, then \emph{uḷḷē} and \emph{veḷiyē} — the wall, and its two sides
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{kaṭṭil}, then read \textbf{\ta{மேசை}}, then say \emph{suvar}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ta{சுவர்} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}A wall\textquotedblright{}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[tarai]{\ta{தரை} (tarai) — the floor}

\label{lesson:TA-C70-floor}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{suvar} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{தரை}}
\textbf{\ta{தரை}} (\emph{tarai}) — \textquotedblleft{}the floor\textquotedblright{}.

The floor — and also the ground outside. Tamil does not need two words for it; what is under your feet is \ta{தரை} wherever you are standing.

This is where the \ta{கோலம்} (\emph{kōlam}) is drawn each morning, just inside the \ta{வாசல்}. Both of those words are already yours, and this is the one that was missing to put them in a place.

It ends in the \textbf{\ta{ை}} again — the fifth word in three chapters to do so.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four, and the room has a bottom.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{tarai}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{kōlam}, then \emph{vāsal}, then \emph{tarai} — and say where the design is drawn
  \item \emph{Recall:} read \textbf{\ta{மேசை}}, then say \emph{suvar}, then say \emph{tarai}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where is the \ta{கோலம்} drawn? (On the \textbf{\ta{தரை}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kūrai]{\ta{கூரை} (kūrai) — a roof}

\label{lesson:TA-C70-roof}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{tarai} mean, and what did \emph{suvar} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{கூரை}}
\textbf{\ta{கூரை}} (\emph{kūrai}) — \textquotedblleft{}a roof\textquotedblright{}.

The roof over you.

With \ta{தரை} under your feet and \ta{கூரை} over your head, the room has both ends — and you already have the two words for the space between them: \ta{மேலே} and \ta{கீழே}. Point up at the \ta{கூரை}, down at the \ta{தரை}, and every word in that sentence is one you have been taught.

Its \textbf{\ta{ூ}} is the long u sign, and it ends, like \ta{தரை}, in \textbf{\ta{ை}}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five: a table, a bed, a wall, a floor and a roof.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{kūrai}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{mēlē}, then \emph{kūrai}; \emph{kīḻē}, then \emph{tarai}
  \item \emph{Say it:} all five — \emph{mēsai}, \emph{kaṭṭil}, \emph{suvar}, \emph{tarai}, \emph{kūrai}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{suvar}, then say \emph{tarai}, then say \emph{kūrai}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which of the five is \ta{மேலே}, and which is \ta{கீழே}? (\textbf{\ta{கூரை}}; \textbf{\ta{தரை}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
